opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I really want from benchmarks like WebShop is for them to pull the field toward tasks that look like the real world. For a long time, a lot of our benchmarks in reinforcement learning were games, which were great for making progress on decision-making, but they sat pretty far from anything a person actually needs done. With WebShop, the idea was simple: someone gives you a natural-language description of a product they want, and the agent has to search, browse through pages, reason about options, pick the right attributes, and actually complete the purchase. It's mundane, but that's the point. It combines language understanding with sequential decision-making, in an environment that's messy and open-ended the way real tasks are.

The second thing I care about is measurement. If a benchmark is going to be useful, it should give you a clear, automatic, reproducible score, without a human having to judge each run and without the task being so narrow that you can game it. It should also be hard enough to expose where agents are failing, whether that's in planning, in exploring when the first search doesn't work, or in recovering from a mistake. A single final number matters less than whether the benchmark tells you something about why the agent fell short. Otherwise, you end up with demos that look impressive but don't tell you much.

Ultimately, I want these benchmarks to act as a kind of bridge between research and deployment. A good one tells researchers what to work on next, and it gives people building products some evidence of whether an agent can be trusted with a task. Benchmarks also have a shelf life. As models get better, the old ones saturate, and you need to keep raising the bar toward longer tasks, more complex environments, and things like reliability and cost, rather than just asking whether the agent succeeded once. So the goal is less about having a leaderboard and more about steering the whole community toward the capabilities that will actually matter when these systems are out in the world.

r001.rationale: The response advocates benchmarks built around tasks people actually need done and contrasts WebShop’s realistic, open-ended shopping task with games.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks saturate as models improve and calls for raising the bar, conveying that existing benchmarks can cap what they reveal about stronger models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is: I want benchmarks like WebShop to force us to confront the problems that real deployment forces on you, instead of the ones that are convenient to study.

A lot of the earlier agent work, including some of my own, lived in grid worlds or text games where the environment was clean and small. That was useful for developing ideas, but it let us dodge the hard parts. The web is messy. Pages are long, full of noise, the product catalog is enormous, the instructions people give are underspecified, and you have to actually read, navigate, and commit to a decision. When we built WebShop, we took real product data, over a million items, and real-ish instructions from people, and the point was to make a language model do the whole loop: understand what the user wants, search, browse, compare attributes, and buy the right thing.

So I'd say there are three things I want from it. First, grounding. The agent has to tie language to actions in an actual environment where its choices have consequences, not just produce plausible text. Second, a gap that's honest. Humans do very well on WebShop, and models at the time did quite a bit worse, and that gap tells you something true about where the models fall short, whether it's long-horizon planning, or recovering from a bad search, or reading tables. Third, transferability. We showed that policies trained on WebShop could be pointed at real Amazon and eBay with some success, which, for me, is the real test of whether a benchmark means anything. If what you learn in the sandbox doesn't carry over, you've optimized for the sandbox.

And then there's the thing I care about most, which is that a good benchmark should be a bit of a moving target for the research community. It should be hard enough that people try genuinely different approaches, so you get something like ReAct, where reasoning and acting interleave, coming out of the attempt to do better. If a benchmark just gets saturated by scale in a year, it did its job and you move on. The goal isn't the leaderboard, it's the behaviors you had to invent to climb it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts clean, small grid worlds and text games with messy real-world deployment, and says benchmarks should confront those deployment problems.

r002.rationale: It describes models performing worse than humans on WebShop, but does not say current benchmarks impose a ceiling below what models can achieve.

astra-6.text:
I want these benchmarks to tell us whether an agent can take a goal expressed in language and actually carry it out. Shopping is a useful setting because you have to understand what someone wants, search for options, compare them, and make a choice under constraints. It’s not just about generating a plausible answer; your actions have to lead to a useful outcome.

And I’d like benchmarks to help us understand where things break down. Did the agent misunderstand the request? Did it fail to find the right information? Or did it find the information but make the wrong decision? The goal is to measure progress toward agents that can handle new tasks reliably, rather than just get better at a fixed set of examples.

r001.rationale: The response presents shopping as a setting where agents must search, compare options, and choose under constraints to achieve a useful outcome, advocating evaluation on practical tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that current benchmarks cap performance below what models can achieve.

sol-6.1.text:
What we want is a way to measure whether an agent can take a high-level goal and actually carry it out in an environment. In WebShop, you might ask for a particular kind of product with several constraints and a budget. The agent has to search, look at the results, read product descriptions, and make a choice. So it’s testing more than whether the model can give a plausible answer—it has to take actions that lead to a successful outcome.

The broader goal is to have a controlled setting where we can compare approaches and understand where they fail. Can the agent follow the instructions? Can it use what it observes to decide what to do next? Can it recover when a search doesn’t work? Ideally, progress on those capabilities translates into agents that can help people with real tasks.

r001.rationale: The response describes evaluating agents on a constrained shopping task that requires searching, reading descriptions, and making a choice, and says those capabilities should translate to real tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not say current benchmarks cap performance below what models can achieve.
